doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Sitting in with Cannonball's Army band at Fort Knox
summary: Walking guard duty, hearing a band, sitting in in combat boots and impressing Cannonball.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: You know, strange you mention that because this last week, Verve Records called me and sent me two cassettes they’re going to re-issue. They bought the catalogue I think, the old catalogue from Mercury on those sides that we did that you’re talking about and they’re going to put them out in a double CD. And they sent them to me to listen to and clarify like some of the, there were a lot of errors as far as composer credits, and that’s why they sent them to me along with the sheet with the thing on it, which I had those records once, I had them in vinyl. A couple of them I got back because Mercury re-issued a couple of them themselves. But it was really great to hear them again, you know, like a nostalgia. It’s going to be two CDs featuring like three albums, “Cannonball’s Sharp Shooters,” and Nat’s album “To The Ivy League” and there was one more “Cannonball En Route” I think is the name of it. But anyway, I was in the Army with those guys. And that’s a funny story too. I couldn’t get into the Army band because I didn’t play a marching instrument. You know back then to get into the Army band you had to play a marching instrument. So I was slated to go to Korea. So the basic training you know, they give you a rifle, an empty rifle, and they teach you how to walk the guard duty. So the post they assigned me was around the service club. And while I’m walking around it, I hear this great music. I said wow, some fantastic records. You know I just assumed it was records, I wouldn’t expect to hear anything like that on an Army post. And I would walk slow every time I got past the time I got near where the music was coming from. I’d walk very slowly. And you know the way you walk guard duty now I mean you walk two hours and rest one hour. And I said well during my rest period, I’m going to listen to some music, because I was I guess in about my sixth week of basic training. And the only thing I heard musically was five o’clock in the morning these hillbillies waking up with these twanging guitars and transistor radios, and fights breaking out, “Turn that stuff off!” So anyway, when my rest period came I ran back to the service club, and when I ran inside I looked and there is this big band sitting on the stage with this roly poly guy leading it, playing alto. I stopped and I was frozen. I listened and I just ran up to the stage then and I listened to a couple of tunes. And something I’d never do is ask to sit in. I always wait to be asked you know. But then I couldn’t hold back. I says, “Hey man, could I sit in with the band?” So the piano player, I was standing near him and he heard me. So he reaches down off the stage and pulls me up and says, “Hey yeah man, play.” And he disappeared. Now the piano player was a clarinet player who just knew some piano chords. And he had a date in Louisville. This was in Fort Knox, Kentucky. And he was late for his date, having to play this gig. So he disappeared. So there I am sitting there, they’ve all got civvies on, because you know, during the Korean War in the States, after four o’clock

you could put your civilian clothes on, on any Army post in the States (not overseas). But I’m sitting there, you know I’m walking guard duty with combat boots, helmet, cartridge belt, and so Cannonball’s giving me like such a look of disdain, I’ve never seen in my life, like wow, who is this cat? And the rest of the guys in the band are looking like, “Huh?” So Cannonball asked, he says, “What do you want to play?” I says, “Well play anything out of your book.” And by saying it like that, you know, that kind of caught him. It kind of surprised him, like maybe the guy is a musician. So they called an easy tune, an easy bebop tune with blues changes. They played the head and then they gave me the first solo. Cannonball says, “All right you got it.” I said what did he say that for, you know I haven’t been near a piano in six weeks. I just played and I stretched out and he started, “Yeah man, play some more.” And I looked, and I happened to look up at the rest of the band and I see heads going like that. And after a while they say, “Yeah, yeah man, go ahead, go ahead.” I must have made about nine choruses. Then the band came in and I read the charts and all. And so after that was over, Cannonball comes over to the piano and says, “Yeah man, that’s great, what’s your name?” I say, “Junior Mance.” And Sonny Stitt was one of his heroes man, and I had worked with Sonny and Gene before I got drafted. Sonny Stitt and Gene Ammons. So he says, he laughs, he says, “If you’re Junior Mance what are you doing here in those clothes?” I said, “What are you doing here?”
Nobody was there by choice, right?
